result.summary: A set of short fragments from the Catalogue of Women. They cover kinship (Patroclus, Asclepius's parentage, Serus), the daughters of Tyndareus whom Aphrodite shames, and the suitors who came to woo Helen.

scenes.title: Kinship notes: Patroclus and Serus
scenes.summary: Ancient commentators cite Hesiod on Menoethius as Peleus's brother, and on Serus and Alazygus, sons of Halirrhothius and Alcyone.

scenes.title: Parentage of Asclepius
scenes.summary: Scholars dispute whether Asclepius was son of Arsinoe or Coronis. Verses attributed to Hesiod name Arsinoe as mother by Apollo.

scenes.title: Scattered notes: Cyclopes, Echemus, Helen
scenes.summary: Brief citations: the Cyclopes destroyed by Apollo, Timandra wed to Echemus, Castor and Polydeuces as sons of Zeus, and Helen as daughter of Ocean and Zeus.

scenes.title: Aphrodite shames Tyndareus's daughters
scenes.summary: Aphrodite, angered at Tyndareus, makes his daughters desert their husbands: Timandra, Clytaemnestra and Helen.
scenes.stakes: The daughters' reputations are ruined by Aphrodite's jealousy.

scenes.title: The suitors of Helen
scenes.summary: Many heroes, including Philoctetes, the sons of Amphiaraus and Odysseus, seek Helen. Odysseus sends no gifts, knowing Menelaus will win, and Agamemnon woos for Menelaus.
scenes.stakes: Suitors risk losing Helen to a rival; Helen's marriage is to be decided.

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: Links Timandra, Clytaemnestra and Helen as faithless sisters through Aphrodite's anger.
Shows Odysseus's shrewdness in declining to bid for Helen.

analysis.text: The fragments concern genealogy and marriage, the Catalogue's main subject, showing how heroic lineages interlock and how divine anger shapes women's fates.
The citations by scholiasts show how ancient scholars debated attributions and local variants, such as Messenian claims for Asclepius.

legacy.text: The catalogue of Helen's suitors helped shape the later tradition of the suitors' oath to Tyndareus, which explained the Greek expedition to Troy.

fun_facts.text: Fragment 68 survives on a Berlin papyrus, with gaps marked as lacunae, so the Helen suitor list is incomplete.

language_notes.text: Eustathius was a 12th-century Byzantine archbishop who wrote commentaries on Homer; "first cousins" follows from Menoethius and Peleus being brothers.
A scholiast is an ancient or medieval commentator whose notes were written in the margins of a classical text.
"Interpolators" are later writers who inserted verses into a poem and passed them off as the original author's work.
"Phoebus" is a title of Apollo, meaning "bright"; "subject in love" means she yielded to him in love.
"Son of Zeus and Leto" is a roundabout way of naming Apollo.
The Cyclopes are the one-eyed craftsmen of myth. In one tradition Apollo killed them in revenge for Zeus's killing of his son Asclepius.
"Buxom" here is an old sense meaning pliant, comely or agreeable, not its modern meaning.
The usual story makes Helen the daughter of Zeus and Leda. A rival tradition made Nemesis her mother. Hesiod's version is different from both.
"Cast them into evil report" means gave them a bad reputation, making their names notorious for infidelity.
"Dishonoured the couch" means violated the marriage bed, i.e. committed adultery.
The "dark-faced daughter of Ocean" is Leda's mother-figure here; the text names Zeus and Tyndareus as sharing her embraces, hinting at Helen's divine paternity.
"Perforce" means by force or necessarily; the brothers would have made the suitor their kinsman regardless of his wishes.
The sons of Amphiaraus are Alcmaeon and Amphilochus; Amphiaraus was the seer who died at Thebes.
"Neat-ankled" is a conventional epithet praising a woman's graceful form.

context_notes.text: Patroclus was Achilles' dearest companion in the Iliad. Peleus was Achilles' father.
Pausanias was a 2nd-century AD Greek travel writer. The Messenians claimed Asclepius as a native son of Arsinoe, daughter of a Messenian king.
Asclepius was the god of healing. His parentage was disputed. The more common story makes Coronis his mother, and Arsinoe was the Messenian claim.
Castor and Polydeuces (the Dioscuri) were twin heroes. In some versions Castor is the mortal son of Tyndareus, so Hesiod's claim is notable.
Steischorus was a lyric poet of the sixth century BC who retold myths; a scholiast is an ancient commentator whose notes preserve such fragments.
Aphrodite is the goddess of love and desire; neglecting her honours was a typical cause of divine anger.
Philoctetes was the famed archer who later owned the bow of Heracles and fought at Troy.
Menelaus, rich in possessions, eventually won Helen; the suitors' wooing-gifts were a normal part of Greek marriage negotiation.

literary_notes.text: Stock descriptive phrases such as "leader of men" and "with the lovely hair" are typical of Hesiodic and Homeric epic style.
The commentator uses a question to point out an apparent inconsistency, as a way of arguing against the poet's attribution.
"Laughter-loving" is Aphrodite's stock epithet, ironically set against her vindictive jealousy here.
The repeated "even so" lines up three sisters' desertions in parallel, making the pattern of scandal feel inevitable.
Helen's beauty is compared to golden Aphrodite and the Graces, ironic given Aphrodite's anger at her family.
Odysseus is shown as shrewd: he saves his gifts because he calculates the outcome, foreshadowing his cunning in the epics.
